To rescind something means to officially cancel, withdraw, or take back a decision, agreement, law, or order that was previously made — as if it never existed or as if it no longer holds any power.

Think of it this way: when you rescind something, you are undoing an official act. You put something into place, and now you are pulling it back out.
The Key Idea: It Has to Be Something "Official"

This is the most important thing to understand about "rescind." You don't rescind casual, everyday things. You rescind things that carry formal authority or weight — things like:

  • A law or regulation
  • A job offer
  • A contract
  • A policy
  • An order or decree
  • A decision made by a committee, court, or organization
  • A membership or license

So if you told your friend you'd meet them for lunch and then changed your mind, you wouldn't say you rescinded your plan. But if a company sent you a formal job offer letter and then officially withdrew it, they rescinded the offer.

• The government rescinded the law after massive public protests. (The law was cancelled.)
  • The university rescinded her admission after discovering she had lied on her application. (The admission was officially taken back.)
  • The board rescinded its earlier decision and voted again. (They cancelled their previous decision.)
  • After the scandal, his security clearance was rescinded. (It was officially revoked.)

When something is rescinded, it stops being valid or enforceable. The act of rescinding doesn't just pause or freeze something — it eliminates its power and effect. In legal and formal settings especially, rescinding something often means treating it as though it should no longer be recognized or acted upon going forward.

Imagine a government passes a rule. That rule has power — people must follow it. The moment the government rescinds that rule, it loses its power. Done. Gone.

Rescinding often carries a sense of reversal and sometimes consequence. It's not a light or casual action. When something is rescinded, it usually means:

  • Something went wrong (e.g., fraud, a mistake, new circumstances), or
  • Someone in power deliberately changed course, or
  • A situation changed so significantly that the original decision no longer makes sense

So there's usually a reason behind a rescission, and it often affects people in significant ways (you lose a job offer, a law stops applying, a contract dissolves).
How It Differs from Similar Words

Since you want to know this word deeply, it helps to understand how it sits among similar words:

  • Cancel is the broad, everyday word. You can cancel a pizza order, a meeting, a show. Rescind is more formal and specific to official acts.
  • Revoke is very close in meaning and often interchangeable with rescind. However, revoke tends to be used when taking back a privilege or right given to a person (a driver's license is revoked, a permit is revoked). Rescind is broader and more commonly used for decisions, laws, orders, and contracts.
  • Repeal is specifically used for laws and legislation. A law is repealed through a legislative process. While you can also say a law is rescinded, repeal is the more precise legal term for that narrow case.
  • Annul typically means to declare something legally void from the beginning — as though it never existed (commonly used for marriages or contracts). Rescind is similar but doesn't always imply it was invalid from the start — it just means it is being cancelled now.
  • Withdraw is softer and more general. You withdraw an offer in a casual or early-stage sense. Rescind is the formal, official version of withdrawal.

In real life, you'll most often see "rescind" paired with these words:

  • Rescind an offer (especially a job offer)
  • Rescind a contract
  • Rescind a law or policy
  • Rescind an order (executive order, court order)
  • Rescind a decision
  • Rescind approval or authorization
  • Rescind membership or accreditation

To rescind = to officially cancel or take back a formal decision, agreement, or rule, stripping it of its power or validity.

If you remember that one line and the idea that it always involves something official, you'll use and understand this word correctly every single time.
